Andrew Ross Sorkin on the Crash of 1929 & The Parallels We See Today | The Real Eisman Playbook

Andrew Ross Sorkin discusses the human incentives and policy failures surrounding 1929. Eisman emphasizes leverage, shared institutional exposures, short-selling survival and the danger of assuming officials already understand a crisis. This is mainly historical explanation, not a prediction of another crash. Original Fed records contradict the guest's assertion that policymakers could not contemplate rate increases in 1929, and preexisting bank capital rules qualify the repeated no-rules narrative.

Conditional reasoning

With equity equal to one tenth of assets, a 10% asset-price decline erases initial equity before interest and transaction costs. A small margin deposit therefore magnifies both gains and losses.

  • An asset position is financed with debt fixed in nominal amount.
  • Equity is the residual asset value less debt.

Conditional reasoning

An investor forced to close during an interim rise realizes a loss and cannot benefit from the subsequent fall. Forecast direction alone therefore does not guarantee a profitable executable trade.

  • A short position faces interim mark-to-market losses, margin limits, borrow costs or recall risk.
  • Prices can rise before a later decline.

The conditional relationship follows from the explicit assumptions; it does not establish that those assumptions hold in observed markets.

Qualification: This is a conditional risk framework. The rhetorical assertion that derivatives are the only difference between historical crises is not endorsed.

Conditional reasoning

Common asset losses erode capital; forced deleveraging depresses asset prices further and unmet funding obligations spread stress. Derivative exposures can add contingent obligations to this mechanism.

  • Leveraged institutions have capital small relative to exposed assets.
  • Several important institutions share exposure and have interconnected funding obligations.

How he reasons here

  • Map leverage, shared assets and funding links before calling a downturn systemic.
  • Separate correct bearish direction from the ability to survive a short.
  • Do not assume policymakers possess all available information or can act promptly.
  • Distinguish the crash, the ensuing depression, the start of recovery and full employment.
  • Use historical analogies as risk prompts rather than deterministic forecasts.
  • Check original policy actions before inferring motives from a narrative.
